title: THE BYSTANDER EFFECT
paras: In March 1964, a young woman named Kitty Genovese was attacked outside her apartment building in New York. According to a newspaper report published two weeks later, thirty-eight neighbours heard her cries for help, yet none of them intervened or even called the police until it was too late. The story shocked the nation and raised a disturbing question: how could so many people witness an emergency and do nothing? Later investigations showed that the original report had exaggerated the number of witnesses, but the case nonetheless inspired one of the most influential research programmes in social psychology.

Two psychologists, John Darley and Bibb Latané, suspected that the neighbours' passivity was not caused by indifference or moral weakness. Instead, they proposed that the very presence of other people might discourage individuals from helping. They called this phenomenon the bystander effect: the more witnesses there are to an emergency, the less likely it is that any single one of them will offer help. This idea ran against common sense, since most people assume that a victim is safer in a crowd than with a single passer-by.

To test their hypothesis, Darley and Latané (1968) designed an experiment in which university students took part in what they believed was a discussion about personal problems. Each participant sat alone in a booth and communicated with the others through an intercom. Some participants were told that they were talking to one other person, while others believed that the group consisted of three or six people. In reality, all the other voices were pre-recorded. During the discussion, one of the voices began to suffer what sounded like a serious seizure and called for help.

The results were striking. When participants believed that they were the only ones who could hear the victim, 85 percent left their booth to look for help before the seizure ended. When they believed that four other people were also listening, only 31 percent did so. Moreover, those who did help in larger groups took considerably longer to react. Interestingly, the participants who failed to act did not appear indifferent; on the contrary, many of them were sweating and trembling when the experimenter entered their booth, which suggests that they were in a state of conflict rather than apathy.

Darley and Latané explained these findings with the concept of diffusion of responsibility. When a person is the only witness, the responsibility to act falls entirely on him or her. However, when several people are present, the responsibility is shared among them, so each individual feels less personally obliged to intervene. Each bystander may also assume that someone else has already called for help, and as a result, nobody does.

A second process that contributes to the bystander effect is pluralistic ignorance. Emergencies are often ambiguous: a man lying on the pavement may be ill, but he may also simply be sleeping. In such situations, people look at the reactions of others to decide how to interpret the event. (A) Since everyone tries to appear calm in public, each person sees that the others are not alarmed. (B) Consequently, the whole group may conclude that nothing serious is happening. (C) In one well-known study, participants who were filling out questionnaires in a room that gradually filled with smoke were far less likely to report it when they were sitting with two calm strangers than when they were alone. (D)

A third factor is evaluation apprehension, that is, the fear of being judged by others. Helping in public carries a social risk: a person who rushes to assist someone who does not actually need help may look foolish. The larger the audience, the greater this fear becomes, so potential helpers may hesitate in order to avoid embarrassment. Taken together, these three processes show that the bystander effect is less a matter of bad character than of the way people think and behave in groups.

The bystander effect, however, is not inevitable. Later research has identified several conditions under which people are more willing to help even when others are present. For instance, bystanders are more likely to intervene when the emergency is clearly dangerous, when they know the victim personally, or when they feel competent to deal with the situation. A nurse, for example, is less affected by the number of onlookers than an ordinary passer-by because she knows exactly what to do. Similarly, people who belong to the same social group as the victim are more inclined to act.

In 2019, a team of researchers led by Richard Philpot challenged the pessimistic picture painted by earlier laboratory studies. Instead of staging artificial emergencies, they analysed real public conflicts recorded by security cameras in three cities: Amsterdam, Cape Town and Lancaster. They found that in nine out of ten incidents, at least one bystander intervened, and the probability of help actually increased as the number of bystanders grew. According to the researchers, the presence of many people does not reduce the chance that the victim will be helped; it simply makes it less likely that any particular person will be the one who helps.

These findings do not necessarily contradict the classic research. Laboratory studies measure the behaviour of an individual, whereas camera footage reveals the outcome for the victim. Therefore, although each witness in a large crowd may be less likely to act, a crowd still contains more potential helpers. Some psychologists argue that the original research was misleading not because its results were wrong, but because it was often presented to the public as evidence that people in cities do not care about one another.

Knowledge of the bystander effect can itself reduce its power. Studies show that people who have learned about diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance are more likely to help in later emergencies. First-aid instructors therefore advise victims to make their requests specific: instead of shouting "Somebody help me!", a person in trouble should point to one individual and say, "You in the blue jacket, call an ambulance." Such a request removes ambiguity and places the responsibility on a single person, thereby turning a passive spectator into an active helper.

notes.d: a sudden attack of illness in which a person cannot control the movements of the body
a lack of interest or concern

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT true according to paragraph 1?
o: The attack on Kitty Genovese took place near her home.
The newspaper report was published shortly after the incident.
Later investigations confirmed that exactly thirty-eight people witnessed the attack.
The case led to a significant area of research in social psychology.
qs.kanit: Later investigations showed that the original report had exaggerated the number of witnesses
qs.why: Metinde sonraki araştırmaların tanık sayısının abartıldığını gösterdiği yazıyor; yani 38 sayısı doğrulanmadı, tersine abartılı bulundu. Diğer seçenekler metinde var: 'outside her apartment building', 'two weeks later', 'inspired one of the most influential research programmes'.

qs.q: Why does the author mention that "most people assume that a victim is safer in a crowd" in paragraph 2?
o: To show that Darley and Latané's idea contradicted a widely held belief
To prove that crowds are more dangerous than individuals
To explain why the neighbours in New York did not call the police
To criticise the public for misunderstanding psychological research
qs.kanit: This idea ran against common sense
qs.why: Yazar, Darley ve Latané'nin fikrinin sağduyuya ters düştüğünü vurgulamak için yaygın inancı hatırlatıyor: 'ran against common sense'. Kalabalığın tehlikeli olduğunu kanıtlamıyor; yalnızca yardım olasılığının düştüğünü söylüyor.

qs.q: In Darley and Latané's experiment, what was the real source of the other voices that participants heard?
qs.kanit: In reality, all the other voices were pre-recorded.
qs.why: Katılımcılar başkalarıyla konuştuklarını sanıyordu ama 'all the other voices were pre-recorded': bütün diğer sesler önceden kaydedilmişti.

qs.q: What can be inferred from the description of the participants who did not help in paragraph 4?
o: They did not notice that the victim was in danger.
They cared about the victim but were unsure whether they should act.
They believed that the seizure was not real.
They were too frightened of the experimenter to leave the booth.
qs.kanit: which suggests that they were in a state of conflict rather than apathy
qs.why: Terleyip titremeleri, kayıtsız olmadıklarını ama ne yapacakları konusunda iç çatışma yaşadıklarını gösteriyor: 'conflict rather than apathy'. Sesin sahte olduğunu bildiklerine ya da deneyciden korktuklarına dair bir bilgi yok.

qs.q: Complete the summary of paragraph 5 with words from the box. There are more words than you need.
qs.ctx: According to the idea of diffusion of responsibility, a single witness carries all the [1] to act. When there are several witnesses, each one feels less [2] to help, and everyone may [3] that someone else has already done something.
qs.kanit: the responsibility is shared among them, so each individual feels less personally obliged to intervene
qs.why: Paragrafta tek tanıkta 'the responsibility to act falls entirely on him or her', kalabalıkta 'feels less personally obliged' ve 'may also assume that someone else has already called for help' ifadeleri var.

qs.q:
There is a missing sentence in paragraph 6. Where does the following sentence fit best?
"In other words, each individual uses the calm behaviour of the others as evidence that there is no emergency."
qs.kanit: Since everyone tries to appear calm in public, each person sees that the others are not alarmed.
qs.why: 'In other words' bir önceki cümleyi başka sözlerle açıklar. Önceki cümle herkesin sakin göründüğünü ve diğerlerinin endişelenmediğini söylüyor; eksik cümle bunu 'kanıt' olarak yorumladıklarını açıklıyor. Ardından gelen 'Consequently' de bu sonuca bağlanıyor, bu yüzden yer (B).

qs.q: According to paragraph 8, which TWO of the following would make a bystander MORE likely to help?
o: The bystander has medical training.
There are very few other witnesses.
The victim is a friend of the bystander.
The situation does not look dangerous.
The bystander is in a hurry.
qs.kanit: when they know the victim personally, or when they feel competent to deal with the situation
qs.why: Paragraf yardımı artıran koşulları sayıyor: tehlikenin açık olması, kurbanı tanımak ve kendini yetkin hissetmek (hemşire örneği). Tanık sayısının azlığı paragrafta bir koşul olarak geçmiyor; tehlikesiz görünmek ise yardımı azaltır.

qs.q: How does paragraph 9 relate to the earlier paragraphs?
o: It provides further laboratory evidence that supports Darley and Latané's findings.
It presents real-world evidence that questions the negative conclusions of earlier studies.
It explains the psychological processes behind the bystander effect in more detail.
It shows that the bystander effect only exists in large cities.
qs.kanit: challenged the pessimistic picture painted by earlier laboratory studies
qs.why: Philpot'un ekibi yapay deneyler yerine gerçek kamera kayıtlarını inceledi ve önceki çalışmaların karamsar tablosuna meydan okudu ('challenged the pessimistic picture'). Bu laboratuvar kanıtı değil, gerçek dünya kanıtı.

qs.q: A woman faints at a crowded train station. Many people stop and look at each other, and since nobody seems worried, they continue walking. Which process from the text BEST explains this situation?
o: Diffusion of responsibility
Pluralistic ignorance
Evaluation apprehension
Social group membership
qs.kanit: people look at the reactions of others to decide how to interpret the event
qs.why: İnsanlar durumu yorumlamak için birbirlerinin tepkisine bakıyor ve kimse endişeli görünmediği için ciddi bir şey olmadığına karar veriyor. Bu, paragraf 6'daki çoğulcu bilgisizlik (pluralistic ignorance).

qs.q: According to the last paragraph, a person who needs help should make a specific request because it removes ambiguity and ____________.
a: places the responsibility on a single person
puts the responsibility on one person
qs.kanit: Such a request removes ambiguity and places the responsibility on a single person
qs.why: Belirli bir kişiye seslenmek hem belirsizliği ortadan kaldırıyor hem de sorumluluğu tek bir kişiye yüklüyor.
